idiom_name: generated gRPC client (forwarder) plus service base (receiver); Socket + System.IO.Pipelines elsewhere
implementation_notes: .NET's mainstream answer is a generated RPC client: the gRPC tooling turns a .proto contract into a typed client whose async method call marshals the request and ships it over GrpcChannel.ForAddress (the channel is the name-to-address step), and into a GreeterBase-derived class whose method is invoked after unmarshalling on the service side - the forwarder and receiver are generated code, and the peer never sees the transport. Where the wire format is fixed by a legacy peer, the roles are assembled from Socket/TcpClient with a System.IO.Pipelines loop: PipeWriter/PipeReader with ReadOnlySequence<byte> give buffering and back-pressure without hand-written byte shuttling, and a length prefix replaces the classic envelope header. The full hand-written structure (own codec plus own receiver loop) is justified only when the protocol cannot be generated and must stay byte-compatible.
pitfalls: Generated gRPC clients are thread-safe and meant to be long-lived: constructing one per call leaks channels and ports.
On the hand-rolled path the Pipe must be completed in every exit path (CompleteAsync), or a peer read hangs forever after a disconnect.
With a raw Socket every ReceiveAsync result must be checked - a partial line is the norm, not the exception - and protobuf's silent skipping of unknown fields can hide schema drift.
